newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Key industries to benefit from election.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Key industries to benefit from election.

text.p: A U.S. government locked in bipartisan struggle presided over one of history's strongest bull markets, and Wall Street expects key industries will benefit from that continuing trend after Tuesday's election.
High techs, drugs and tobaccos are the winners in the U.S. elections, benefiting both from President Bill Clinton's reelection and the continuing Republican hold on Congress.

"We are in a realistic, pragmatic government environment," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "This will be another improvisational administration without any strong ideological bent either way. It's what the business world likes."

Winners among individual industries include the high technologies, with Clinton promising broader access to the internet, and consumer-oriented companies which will benefit from continued slow growth, Wall Street analysts said.

"The President said that he would connect the classrooms of America to the internet. For that, you will need a lot of computers, semiconductors and software," said Kenneth Mayland, chief economist at KeyCorp. He said this was positive for the likes of Microsoft Corp, Intel Corp and on-line companies.
"There are lots of little proposals designed to promote the technologies, which are doing well anyway," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.

Consumer-oriented companies such as food and beverage makers, drugs and tobaccos will also continue to benefit from the slow growth environment, which will shift money away from capital goods type companies.
"Republican control of Congress is beneficial to healthcare and pharmaceutical companies because a nationalized healthcare system will be a non-starter for the next two years," Mayland said.
"As much as the administration would like another shot at it, it just won't happen with a Republican Congress."
Drug and healthcare stocks sold of sharply in 1993 and 1994 amid fears that the Clinton administration's sweeping health care reform plan would have sharply cut back their earnings potential.
Tobacco stocks are helped in much the same way. Clinton has been hostile to the interests of tobacco companies but things could have been much worse.

The reelection of pro-tobacco Republican Senators Jesse Helms on North Carlolina and Strom Thurmond of South Carolina will throw a wrench into any Democratic efforts to further regulate the sale of cigarettes, analysts said.

"Clinton can try, but Congress is not on his side for the most part," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. But he said the advance for stocks like Philip Morris Cos Inc would be capped by ongoing fears of lawsuits despite its rally after the election.

"The stock is undervalued because of the issue of the liability of the tobacco companies," Bleier said. "These stocks may rally in the near term, but they are limited by the belief of investors that one day they will have to pay."
Basic industries and consumer cyclicals such as chemicals, aluminum, autos and airlines will have a less easy time of it, First Albany's Johnson said.
"If you have a slow economy, you want to buy the stock of companies which will produce earnings year in and year out in such an economy," Johnson said.
"People will buy, toothpaste and food and soft drinks but will sacrifice making airplane trips or buying a car," he said.
